subject: Mixed (Real Weightage)
description: Full 100-question mock exam following the REAL PGP-CET 2025 topic weightage (per the official exam brochure), sourced entirely from uploaded reference books with citations.

questions.question: Madelung's deformity results from retarded growth of which structure?

options.A: The lower end of the radius
options.B: The upper end of the humerus
options.C: The olecranon process of the ulna
options.D: The scaphoid tubercle

questions.explanation: Madelung's deformity is a dorsal subluxation (displacement) of the lower end of the ulna, caused by retarded growth of the lower end of the radius.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: After a fracture of both the radius and ulna shafts, why must cross-union (bony union between the two bones) be specifically prevented during healing?

options.A: Cross-union has no functional consequence
options.B: Cross-union would permanently fuse the radius and ulna together, abolishing pronation and supination of the hand
options.C: Cross-union only affects elbow flexion, not the hand
options.D: It increases the risk of scaphoid fracture

questions.explanation: Pronation and supination depend on the radius being able to rotate around a stable ulna. If the two bones heal fused together (cross-union), that rotation becomes impossible, so surgeons take specific care during fixation of combined radius-ulna shaft fractures to prevent it.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: The lateral surface of the pisiform bone is grooved by which structure?

options.A: The radial artery
options.B: The median nerve
options.C: The ulnar nerve
options.D: The tendon of flexor carpi radialis

questions.explanation: The lateral surface of the pisiform is grooved by the ulnar nerve as it passes into the hand through Guyon's canal, alongside the ulnar artery.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Carpal Bones

questions.question: The ulna is often described as the 'stabilising bone' of the forearm because:

options.A: Its trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus, giving the radius a stable foundation from which to pronate and supinate
options.B: It is the only bone that moves during pronation/supination
options.C: It bears the entire weight of the upper limb at the wrist joint
options.D: It has no muscular attachments, unlike the radius

questions.explanation: The ulna's trochlear notch grips the lower end of the humerus at the elbow, forming a stable hinge. This gives the radius the fixed foundation it needs to rotate around the ulna for efficient pronation and supination of the hand.
questions.sourceBook: BD Chaurasia's Human Anatomy — Upper Limb
questions.sourceChapter: Bones of the Upper Limb — Clinical Anatomy

questions.question: The Gibbs-Donnan membrane equilibrium describes what happens when a membrane permeable to some ions separates two solutions, one of which also contains a non-diffusible (non-penetrating) ion such as a protein anion. What is the key consequence?

options.A: All ions distribute exactly equally on both sides regardless of the non-diffusible ion
options.B: The diffusible ions distribute asymmetrically at equilibrium — the diffusible cation concentration is higher on the side containing the non-penetrating anion
options.C: The non-diffusible ion eventually crosses the membrane too, given enough time
options.D: No electrical potential difference develops across the membrane

questions.explanation: When a non-diffusible anion (like a protein) is confined to one side, the freely diffusible ions (like K+ and Cl-) redistribute asymmetrically at equilibrium to maintain electrical neutrality and equal ion products on both sides — the diffusible cation ends up more concentrated on the side with the trapped anion. This asymmetry is the Gibbs-Donnan equilibrium and contributes to the resting membrane potential.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Gibbs-Donnan Membrane Equilibrium

questions.question: Why does ischaemia (reduced blood/oxygen supply) lead to cell swelling and damage?

options.A: Ischaemia has no effect on the Na+-K+ pump
options.B: Ischaemia decreases Na+-K+ pump activity, disrupting osmotic equilibrium and allowing the cell to swell
options.C: Ischaemia directly ruptures the cell membrane through mechanical force
options.D: Ischaemia only affects extracellular fluid, never intracellular volume

questions.explanation: The Na+-K+ pump normally keeps osmotic equilibrium by moving positive charge (and effectively solute) out of the cell, counteracting the tendency of intracellular protein anions and other molecules to draw water in and cause swelling. Ischaemia reduces the ATP-dependent pump's activity, disrupting this balance — which is why prolonged cerebral ischaemia, causing cell swelling and damage, is often fatal.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Gibbs-Donnan Effect

questions.question: Although sodium's atomic weight (23) is lower than potassium's (39), Na+ moves through the resting cell membrane with greater difficulty than K+. Why?

options.A: Sodium ions carry a different electrical charge than potassium
options.B: Ions in body fluids are hydrated, and the hydrated Na+ ion is actually larger in radius than the hydrated K+ ion
options.C: Sodium is chemically unable to pass through any biological membrane
options.D: Potassium is not actually present in body fluids at rest

questions.explanation: Ions in solution are hydrated (surrounded by a shell of water molecules). Despite its lower atomic weight, hydrated Na+ has a larger effective radius than hydrated K+, which is a key reason Na+ crosses the resting membrane with more difficulty than K+.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Introduction, Size of Hydrated Ions

questions.question: The Na+-K+ pump is described as 'electrogenic at rest' because it operates with a coupling ratio of 3 Na+ out for every 2 K+ in. What would happen to its contribution to the membrane potential if the coupling ratio were instead 1:1?

options.A: It would generate an even larger membrane potential
options.B: It would not directly generate any membrane potential itself, though it would still maintain the concentration gradients the potential depends on
options.C: The cell would immediately depolarise completely and stay depolarised
options.D: The pump would stop functioning altogether

questions.explanation: At a 3:2 coupling ratio, the Na+-K+ pump moves net positive charge out of the cell with each cycle, directly contributing a small electrogenic component to the membrane potential. If the ratio were 1:1 (equal charge moved each way), the pump itself would not generate any net potential directly — though it would still be essential for maintaining the ionic concentration gradients that the resting membrane potential fundamentally depends on.
questions.sourceBook: AK Jain, Physiology
questions.sourceChapter: The Membrane Potentials — Genesis of Resting Membrane Potential

questions.question: A dipeptide, formed from two amino acids, contains how many peptide bonds?

options.A: Zero
options.B: One
options.C: Two
options.D: Three

questions.explanation: A dipeptide has two amino acids joined by exactly one peptide bond — a common point of confusion, since it's easy to assume 'two amino acids' implies 'two bonds.'
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Peptide Bond

questions.question: What is the key limitation of Sanger's reagent (1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene) compared to Edman's reagent for determining a protein's amino acid sequence?

options.A: It only works on carbohydrates, not proteins
options.B: After labelling the N-terminal residue, the protein must be fully hydrolysed to identify it — destroying the polypeptide and preventing repeated sequencing cycles
options.C: It cannot label any amino acid at all
options.D: It is more expensive but otherwise functionally identical to Edman's reagent

questions.explanation: Sanger's reagent labels the free N-terminal amino group, but identifying that labelled residue requires complete hydrolysis of the protein — destroying it in the process. This makes it useful only for identifying the N-terminal residue once, unlike Edman degradation which can be repeated.
questions.sourceBook: Satyanarayana, Biochemistry
questions.sourceChapter: Proteins and Amino Acids — Determination of Primary Structure

questions.question: Which of the following is a documented benefit of Continuous Passive Motion (CPM) following joint surgery?

options.A: A permanent increase in muscle strength
options.B: Increased synovial fluid lubrication and a stimulating effect on healing of cartilage, tendons, and ligaments
options.C: It removes the need for any active exercise afterward
options.D: Guaranteed prevention of postoperative infection

questions.explanation: Documented benefits of CPM include increased synovial fluid lubrication (supporting cartilage healing), a stimulating effect on tendon and ligament healing, prevention of adhesions/contractures, and typically a quicker return of range of motion with less postoperative pain — but it does not replace active exercise or strength training.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Continuous Passive Motion

questions.question: To achieve full passive range of hip flexion, the knee must also be allowed to flex. Why?

options.A: It relaxes tension on the two-joint hamstring muscle group, which would otherwise restrict hip flexion
options.B: It reduces pain in the lumbar spine
options.C: It is required purely to stabilize the pelvis
options.D: Knee position has no real effect on hip flexion range

questions.explanation: The hamstrings cross both the hip and knee. Keeping the knee extended while flexing the hip stretches the hamstrings and limits how far the hip can flex; flexing the knee releases that tension, allowing full hip flexion range to be reached.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Combined Hip and Knee Motion

questions.question: Continuous Passive Motion (CPM) is best described as:

options.A: An exercise in which the patient actively moves a joint against resistance
options.B: A mechanical device that moves a joint slowly and continuously through a controlled range of motion, without effort from the patient
options.C: A manual stretching technique applied by the therapist at end-range
options.D: A functional movement pattern combining several joints at once

questions.explanation: CPM refers specifically to a mechanical device that passively and continuously moves a joint through a set arc of motion, developed following Robert Salter's research into the healing benefits of continual passive movement on joint tissue.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 3: Range of Motion — Continuous Passive Motion

questions.question: 'Passive flexibility' (passive range of motion) is best described as:

options.A: The degree to which an active muscle contraction moves a joint through its available range
options.B: The degree to which a body segment can be moved through its available range by an external force, without the patient contracting the muscle themselves
options.C: The absolute maximum range any joint could reach under general anesthesia
options.D: A measure of muscular endurance during repeated contractions

questions.explanation: Passive flexibility depends on the extensibility of the muscles and connective tissues crossing a joint. It is a prerequisite for, but does not guarantee, dynamic (active) flexibility — which instead depends on the patient's own active muscle contraction moving the segment.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Definition of Terms

questions.question: In a patient with a spinal cord injury who lacks active control of the back extensors, why might a therapist deliberately allow mild hypomobility to develop in the low back extensors while still fully stretching the hamstrings?

options.A: To create a stable, slightly shortened structure the patient can lean into for trunk support during long-term sitting
options.B: Because the back extensors cannot physically be stretched
options.C: To prevent contractures developing in the hamstrings only
options.D: Because stretching the trunk has no clinical value in this population

questions.explanation: This illustrates 'selective stretching': deliberately allowing some hypomobility in muscles the patient cannot actively control (like the back extensors after a thoracic/cervical spinal cord injury) gives them a stable structure to lean into for trunk stability while sitting, while the hamstrings are kept flexible enough for dressing and transfers.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 4: Stretching for Impaired Mobility — Selective Stretching

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Faradic-type currents are typically 'surged' for treatment purposes. What is the purpose of surging the current?

options.A: To reduce the total treatment time
options.B: To produce a near-normal tetanic-like contraction and relaxation of the muscle, by gradually increasing then decreasing the intensity of successive impulses
options.C: To eliminate the need for any electrodes
options.D: To convert the current into direct current permanently

questions.explanation: Surging gradually increases the intensity of successive impulses to a peak, then lets it fall (suddenly or gradually), mimicking a more natural, near-normal tetanic muscle contraction and relaxation cycle rather than an abrupt on/off stimulus.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Modified Faradic Currents

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: For a RISING (increasing) current applied over a superficial nerve, which electrode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse, and why is the active electrode typically connected to it?

options.A: The anode, because it requires less current overall
options.B: The cathode, because it produces contraction of innervated muscle with less current than is required at the anode
options.C: Neither electrode has any different effect
options.D: The anode always requires less current than the cathode

questions.explanation: For a rising current, the cathode is more effective at initiating a nerve impulse than the anode. This is why the active electrode is conventionally connected to the cathode — it produces contraction of innervated muscle using less current than would be needed if the anode were used as the active electrode.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When faradic-type current is applied directly over an innervated muscle, maximum contraction response is generally obtained by stimulating at the:

options.A: Tendon of insertion exclusively
options.B: Motor point — where the main nerve enters the muscle (or, for deep muscles, where it emerges from under more superficial muscles)
options.C: Muscle belly midpoint, regardless of nerve entry
options.D: Origin of the muscle only

questions.explanation: The motor point — the point at which the main nerve supply enters the muscle, or for deeply placed muscles, the point where the nerve emerges from under overlying superficial muscles — is where maximum contraction response is typically obtained with electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Because of accommodation, which type of current change is MORE effective at initiating a nerve impulse: a sudden change, or a gradual one?

options.A: A sudden change in current is more effective than a gradual one
options.B: A gradual change is always more effective
options.C: Both are exactly equally effective in all cases
options.D: Neither a sudden nor gradual change can ever initiate an impulse

questions.explanation: Because the nerve accommodates (adapts) to slowly changing conditions, a current that rises or falls suddenly is more effective at initiating an impulse than one that changes gradually, since gradual change gives the nerve time to accommodate before the threshold is reached.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When beginning faradic stimulation of a muscle group, what is the recommended approach to intensity?

options.A: Start immediately at maximal tolerable intensity
options.B: Give several gentle contractions first to allow the patient to become accustomed to the current, then gradually increase intensity
options.C: Intensity should never be increased throughout the treatment
options.D: Intensity is irrelevant to the treatment outcome

questions.explanation: The recommended approach is to give the patient several gentle contractions first to allow them to become accustomed to the current, then gradually increase the intensity until a strong contraction is achieved — not starting at a high, potentially uncomfortable intensity immediately.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Stimulation of Muscle Groups — Quadriceps

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: In a practical setup for stimulating the quadriceps with a faradic-type current, where is the indifferent (larger) electrode typically placed, per Clayton's described technique?

options.A: Over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle
options.B: Directly over the motor points of the quadriceps only, with no separate indifferent electrode
options.C: On the opposite limb entirely
options.D: Over the lumbar spine

questions.explanation: In the classic technique for faradic stimulation of the quadriceps, one electrode and pad is placed over the femoral nerve in the femoral triangle and secured with a sandbag or bandage, while the other (active) electrode pad is placed across the motor points of the quadriceps.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Stimulation of Muscle Groups — Quadriceps

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: As the frequency of repeated electrical stimuli to a motor nerve increases beyond about 20 Hz, what happens to the muscle's contraction pattern?

options.A: The muscle stops contracting altogether
options.B: There is no longer time for complete relaxation between contractions, producing partial tetany
options.C: Contraction strength decreases progressively to zero
options.D: The muscle contracts only once regardless of how many stimuli are given

questions.explanation: At low stimulation frequencies (e.g. 1 per second), each stimulus produces an isolated twitch with complete relaxation between contractions. As frequency increases, the relaxation period shortens; beyond about 20 Hz there is no longer time for complete relaxation between contractions, producing partial tetany.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Frequency of Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: Impulses with a duration of MORE than 10 ms, often termed interrupted (or modified) direct current, are specifically used to stimulate:

options.A: Normal, innervated muscle via the motor nerve
options.B: Denervated muscle, where the muscle fibres must be stimulated directly (no functioning motor nerve)
options.C: Cardiac muscle exclusively
options.D: Smooth muscle only

questions.explanation: Long-duration impulses (>10 ms), termed interrupted or modified direct current, are used for denervated muscles — since there is no functioning motor nerve, the muscle fibres must be stimulated directly, and these impulses are repeated far less frequently than faradic-type currents (e.g. a 100 ms impulse might be repeated only about 30 times per minute).
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When a MOTOR nerve is electrically stimulated, why does only the downward-travelling (efferent) impulse produce a muscle contraction, while the upward-travelling impulse has no motor effect?

options.A: The upward-travelling impulse is unable to pass the first synapse, since it is travelling in the wrong (antidromic) direction
options.B: The upward-travelling impulse travels faster and arrives too early to have any effect
options.C: Motor nerves cannot conduct impulses in more than one direction under any circumstance
options.D: Only the upward-travelling impulse reaches the muscle

questions.explanation: Stimulating a nerve fibre initiates impulses travelling simultaneously in both directions from the stimulation point. For a motor nerve, the upward (antidromic) impulse cannot pass the first synapse it encounters travelling the 'wrong' way, so it has no effect, while the downward (orthodromic) impulse reaches the muscle normally and causes contraction.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Nerve Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: At what approximate stimulation frequency does a muscle contraction become fully tetanic, with no perceptible relaxation between successive contractions?

options.A: Over 60 Hz
options.B: Under 1 Hz
options.C: Exactly 10 Hz
options.D: Frequency has no relationship to tetany

questions.explanation: As stimulation frequency increases beyond 20 Hz, partial tetany develops; further increases progressively reduce relaxation until, at frequencies over 60 Hz, there is no perceptible relaxation between contractions and the response is fully tetanic.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Effects of Frequency of Stimulation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: 'Accommodation' in nerve physiology refers to the phenomenon whereby:

options.A: A nerve becomes permanently unresponsive after any stimulation
options.B: The nerve adapts to a constant current over time, so that an unvarying (unchanging) current becomes ineffective at initiating an impulse
options.C: Muscle fibres physically move position to avoid the electrode
options.D: Only denervated muscle can show accommodation

questions.explanation: Accommodation is the nerve's adaptation to a constant, unvarying current flow through a mechanism not fully understood — as a result, a current that does not change is not effective at initiating a nerve impulse, which is why intermittent or varying currents are needed for electrical stimulation.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Accommodation

questions.topic: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle
questions.question: When an electrical current stimulates a nerve fibre, the surface of the plasma membrane nearer the cathode becomes:

options.A: More positive, reducing excitability
options.B: More negative relative to the opposite surface, which can reduce the resting potential difference across the membrane on the cathode side and initiate an impulse if it falls enough for sodium permeability to increase
options.C: Completely unaffected by the current
options.D: Permanently depolarised with no possibility of returning to rest

questions.explanation: The membrane surface nearer the cathode becomes more negative. On the side of the nerve nearer the cathode, this additional charge is of opposite polarity to the resting membrane potential, reducing the potential difference (PD) across it — if the PD falls enough for the membrane to become permeable to sodium ions, an impulse is initiated.
questions.sourceBook: Clayton's Electrotherapy
questions.sourceChapter: Electrical Stimulation of Nerve and Muscle — Mechanism of Nerve Stimulation

questions.question: A drug that reacts with an enzyme's catalytic site so strongly (via a covalent bond or very high affinity) that the normal substrate cannot displace it produces which kinetic pattern?

options.A: kM unchanged, Vmax unchanged (no real inhibition)
options.B: kM decreased, Vmax increased
options.C: kM increased and Vmax reduced — a non-equilibrium type of competitive inhibition
options.D: Only Vmax changes while kM decreases proportionally

questions.explanation: Classical competitive inhibition (equilibrium type) raises kM but leaves Vmax unchanged, since enough substrate can still out-compete the inhibitor. But when the inhibitor binds essentially irreversibly at the same catalytic site (e.g. organophosphates on cholinesterase, or methotrexate's very high affinity for dihydrofolate reductase), substrate can no longer displace it — this non-equilibrium type raises kM AND reduces Vmax.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: Which class of receptors produces the fastest onset of response, typically within milliseconds?

options.A: G-protein coupled receptors
options.B: Ligand-gated ion channel receptors
options.C: Transmembrane enzyme-linked receptors
options.D: Nuclear (gene-regulating) receptors

questions.explanation: Ligand-gated ion channel receptors (e.g. nicotinic cholinergic, GABA-A) have the ion channel built directly into the receptor molecule, so agonist binding opens the channel immediately with no intermediate second messenger — giving the fastest response of all receptor types, in milliseconds.
questions.sourceBook: KD Tripathi, Essentials of Medical Pharmacology
questions.sourceChapter: Mechanism of Drug Action; Receptor Pharmacology

questions.question: Among the TORCH agents, which one is most harmful to the fetus specifically when acquired during the first 10 weeks of pregnancy?

options.A: Cytomegalovirus
options.B: Toxoplasma
options.C: Rubella
options.D: Herpes simplex virus

questions.explanation: Rubella (German measles) is teratogenic, and infection during the acute stage of the first 10 weeks of pregnancy is far more harmful to the fetus than infection later in gestation, producing the classic congenital rubella syndrome (ocular defects, cardiac defects, CNS manifestations, sensorineural deafness).
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — TORCH Complex

questions.question: Blastomas (embryomas) such as neuroblastoma, nephroblastoma (Wilms' tumour), and retinoblastoma are notable because they:

options.A: Occur almost exclusively in adults over 60
options.B: Arise from embryonal/partially differentiated cells and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5
options.C: Are always benign despite the '-oma' name
options.D: Only occur in the gonads

questions.explanation: Blastomas arise from embryonal or partially differentiated cells that would normally form the blastema of organs/tissues during embryogenesis, and occur more frequently in infants and children under 5 years of age.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Special Categories of Tumours

questions.question: Plasmodium falciparum causes markedly more severe (malignant) malaria than the other three plasmodial species mainly because:

options.A: It has an exo-erythrocytic stage that the others lack
options.B: It only infects the liver, never red blood cells
options.C: It parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell multiple times, and makes parasitised red cells sticky, causing capillary obstruction in deep organs
options.D: It is transmitted by a different mosquito genus entirely

questions.explanation: Unlike the other plasmodial species (which parasitise only juvenile red cells and lack these features), P. falciparum parasitises red cells of any age, can infect a single red cell with more than one parasite, and makes infected red cells sticky — causing capillary obstruction (e.g. in the brain, producing cerebral malaria) that accounts for its exceptional virulence. It also notably lacks an exo-erythrocytic stage, but that is not the source of its severity.
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Infectious and Parasitic Diseases — Malaria

questions.question: The two basic components present in every tumour (benign or malignant) are the parenchyma and the:

options.A: Supportive stroma
options.B: Basement membrane only
options.C: Necrotic core
options.D: Capsule

questions.explanation: Every tumour has parenchyma (the proliferating tumour cells themselves, which determine the tumour's nature and behaviour) and a supportive stroma (fibrous connective tissue and blood vessels that provide the structural framework for the parenchymal cells to grow on).
questions.sourceBook: Harsh Mohan, Textbook of Pathology
questions.sourceChapter: Neoplasia — Nomenclature and Classification

questions.question: A patient with damage to the RIGHT parietal association cortex draws a clock face but only completes the right half, leaving the left side blank, and is unaware anything is missing. This phenomenon is known as:

options.A: Wernicke's aphasia
options.B: Contralateral neglect
options.C: Prosopagnosia
options.D: Broca's aphasia

questions.explanation: Contralateral neglect is a classic sign of right parietal association cortex damage: patients ignore the left side of space and their own body (the side opposite/contralateral to the damaged hemisphere), often while denying anything is wrong.
questions.sourceBook: Morgan & King, Introduction to Psychology
questions.sourceChapter: Biology of Behavior — Parietal-Lobe Association Cortex

questions.question: The Y-BOCS, a widely used clinical scale for OCD, stands for and is used to:

options.A: Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale — elicit symptoms and rate severity of OCD
options.B: Young-Beck Obsessive Cognition Scale — diagnose depression only
options.C: Yale Behavioural Outcome Classification System — used only in research, never clinically
options.D: A scale exclusively for measuring anxiety, unrelated to OCD

questions.explanation: Y-BOCS stands for the Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale, one of the most useful clinical tools for eliciting the range of obsessive and compulsive symptoms present and rating the overall severity of OCD.
questions.sourceBook: Ahuja, A Short Textbook of Psychiatry
questions.sourceChapter: Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder — Clinical Syndromes

questions.question: When the velocity of a limb movement is held constant by a rate-controlling device during exercise, this is referred to as:

options.A: Isometric contraction
options.B: Isokinetic contraction
options.C: Isotonic contraction only
options.D: Passive contraction

questions.explanation: An isokinetic contraction is one where the velocity of limb movement is held constant by a rate-controlling device (an isokinetic dynamometer), distinguishing it from standard dynamic (isotonic) exercise where velocity is not controlled.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Type of Muscle Contraction

questions.question: Closed-chain exercise is best described as exercise performed:

options.A: In a nonweight-bearing position with the distal segment moving freely
options.B: In a weight-bearing position where the body moves over a fixed distal segment
options.C: Only using free weights, never body weight
options.D: Exclusively with the upper extremity

questions.explanation: Closed-chain exercise is performed in a weight-bearing position, where the body moves over a relatively fixed distal segment (e.g. the foot on the ground during a squat). Open-chain exercise, by contrast, is performed nonweight-bearing, with the distal segment (hand or foot) moving freely.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Position for Exercise

questions.question: When multiple muscle groups are exercised in a single session, the recommended order is generally:

options.A: Small muscle groups before large muscle groups, single-joint before multi-joint exercises
options.B: Large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises
options.C: Order makes no difference to fatigue or training effect
options.D: Lower intensity exercises should always precede higher intensity ones, regardless of warm-up

questions.explanation: The recommended exercise order is large muscle groups before small muscle groups, and multi-joint exercises before single-joint exercises, with higher-intensity exercises performed before lower-intensity ones after an appropriate warm-up.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Exercise Order

questions.question: For a typical healthy but untrained adult beginning a resistance training program, the recommended training zone (percentage of baseline RM) generally falls between:

options.D: There is no established range

questions.explanation: For healthy but untrained adults, a typical training zone falls between 40% and 70% of the baseline RM, with the lower end of the range safer at the start of a program to focus on correct form before progressing intensity.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Training Zone

questions.question: What is the general relationship between the intensity (load) of resistance exercise and the number of repetitions/sets possible?

options.A: There is no relationship — repetitions are independent of load
options.B: An inverse relationship: higher intensity/load permits fewer repetitions and sets, and lower load permits more
options.C: A direct relationship: higher load always allows more repetitions
options.D: Repetitions only depend on the patient's age, never on the load used

questions.explanation: There is an inverse relationship between exercise intensity (load) and the number of repetitions/sets possible — the higher the load, the fewer repetitions and sets that can be performed, and vice versa.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Volume

questions.question: Early strength gains observed in the first 2-3 weeks of a resistance training program are primarily attributed to:

options.A: Actual muscle fiber hypertrophy
options.B: Neural adaptation, since significant hypertrophy/vascularization changes typically require at least 6-12 weeks
options.C: An increase in the total number of muscle fibers (hyperplasia)
options.D: A change in bone density

questions.explanation: Strength gains in the first 2-3 weeks of resistance training are mainly the result of neural adaptation (improved motor unit recruitment and coordination), not muscle tissue change. Significant hypertrophy or increased vascularization typically requires at least 6-12 weeks of consistent training.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Duration

questions.question: When a muscle is immobilized after injury, which muscle fiber type atrophies at a FASTER rate, and what is the clinical implication?

options.A: Type II (fast twitch) fibers atrophy faster, so power training should be prioritized immediately
options.B: Type I (slow twitch) fibers atrophy faster, contributing to faster atrophy of antigravity muscles and underscoring the need for early endurance training
options.C: Both fiber types atrophy at exactly the same rate with immobilization
options.D: Immobilization has no effect on muscle fiber composition

questions.explanation: With immobilization, Type I (slow twitch) fibers atrophy faster than Type II (fast twitch) fibers, and there is also a slow-to-fast fiber type conversion with disuse. Since antigravity (postural) muscles rely heavily on Type I fibers, this contributes to their faster rate of atrophy compared to their antagonists — supporting early initiation of endurance-type training after injury or surgery.
questions.sourceBook: Kisner & Colby, Therapeutic Exercise: Foundations and Techniques
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 6: Resistance Exercise — Muscle Fiber Atrophy

questions.question: In hypospadias, why is ritual/routine circumcision specifically contraindicated in the newborn period?

options.A: Circumcision is never contraindicated in any condition
options.B: The foreskin is often needed later for the surgical reconstruction of the hypospadias
options.C: Hypospadias makes circumcision technically impossible
options.D: It has no bearing on hypospadias management at all

questions.explanation: In hypospadias, the deficient ventral foreskin tissue is often required for the surgical reconstruction of the urethra later on, so removing it via routine circumcision in infancy would compromise the corrective surgery.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Hypospadias

questions.question: A 'retractile' testis is distinguished from a true undescended testis by the fact that:

options.A: A retractile testis can be manipulated without tension into the base of the scrotum, though it is pulled back up by the cremaster muscle
options.B: A retractile testis is always impalpable
options.C: A retractile testis requires orchidopexy immediately
options.D: There is no meaningful difference between the two

questions.explanation: A retractile testis can be brought down to the base of the scrotum without tension, but is then pulled back up by an overactive cremaster reflex — over time it usually resides permanently in the scrotum, though follow-up is still advised as it can rarely re-ascend and require orchidopexy.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Undescended Testes

questions.question: An umbilical hernia in an infant, caused by incomplete closure of the umbilical ring, most commonly:

options.A: Requires emergency surgery at diagnosis
options.B: Resolves spontaneously by around 4 years of age
options.C: Always requires surgical repair within the first month of life
options.D: Is a surgical emergency due to a very high incarceration rate

questions.explanation: Umbilical hernias are common in infants and most resolve spontaneously by around 4 years of age, with incarceration being very rare — unlike supraumbilical hernias, which do not close on their own and are repaired around the same age.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Midline Hernias

questions.question: Orchidopexy for a palpable undescended testis is ideally performed at what age, to optimise fertility outcomes?

options.A: Immediately at birth
options.B: Between 6 and 12 months of age
options.C: Only after puberty
options.D: Age has no bearing on fertility outcomes

questions.explanation: Orchidopexy is ideally performed as a day-case procedure between 6 and 12 months of age. Bringing the testis into the scrotum (below core body temperature) at a young age optimises spermatogenesis and fertility outcomes.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Undescended Testes

questions.question: A child injured by a bicycle handlebar to the abdomen is classically at risk of injury to which structures?

options.A: The urethra and pelvis
options.B: Pancreatic, duodenal, mesenteric, or liver trauma
options.C: The small intestine or lumbar spine only
options.D: Severe crush injury to the chest exclusively

questions.explanation: Handlebar injuries classically cause focal, high-pressure blunt trauma to the upper abdomen, putting the pancreas, duodenum, mesentery, or liver at risk — distinct from lap belt injuries (small intestine/lumbar spine) or straddle injuries (urethra/pelvis).
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — Paediatric Trauma, Patterns of Injury

questions.question: In a child presenting with acute scrotal pain, testicular torsion must be relieved within approximately what time window from symptom onset for a good chance of testicular salvage?

options.A: 6-8 hours
options.B: 48 hours
options.C: 1 week
options.D: There is no time limit

questions.explanation: Testicular torsion must be relieved within 6-8 hours of symptom onset for a good chance of salvaging the testis — this is why any acute scrotum where torsion cannot be confidently excluded requires urgent surgical exploration.
questions.sourceBook: Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery
questions.sourceChapter: Principles of Paediatric Surgery — The Acute Scrotum

questions.question: 'Patient-centred evidence-based medicine' is best defined as:

options.A: Applying research evidence strictly, ignoring the patient's individual circumstances and wishes
options.B: Applying best-available research evidence while taking individual patient factors (clinical and non-clinical, including values and wishes) into account
options.C: A model where patients make all treatment decisions with no clinical input
options.D: Applying guidelines only to patients under 65 years old

questions.explanation: Patient-centred evidence-based medicine combines the best available research evidence with individual patient factors — both clinical (comorbidities, prognosis) and non-clinical (social circumstances, personal values and wishes) — rather than applying guidelines mechanically to every patient.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Patient-Centred Evidence-Based Medicine

questions.question: The concept of a 'treatment threshold' in clinical decision-making primarily balances:

options.A: The doctor's personal preference against the hospital's budget
options.B: The risks of testing/waiting against the risks and benefits of starting treatment now
options.C: Only the cost of the test, with no consideration of patient risk
options.D: Nothing — treatment thresholds do not exist in evidence-based medicine

questions.explanation: The treatment threshold combines the risks of a test, and the risks versus benefits of treatment, to decide the point at which it makes sense to act. For a low-risk, effective intervention (e.g. antibiotics for a likely UTI), the threshold to act is lower; for a high-risk intervention, more diagnostic certainty is required first.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Dealing with Uncertainty

questions.question: The ABCDE approach (Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Disability, Exposure) used in critically ill patients is an example of which error-reduction strategy?

options.A: A clinical prediction rule
options.B: A mnemonic/checklist
options.C: The SBAR communication system
options.D: A cognitive debiasing interview technique

questions.explanation: ABCDE is probably the most widely used mnemonic/checklist in medicine, reducing reliance on fallible memory and ensuring important issues are considered systematically, especially under stress, complexity, or fatigue.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Mnemonics and Checklists

questions.question: A clinician decides to keep a patient in hospital 'just in case', despite evidence-based guidelines and a completed systematic assessment supporting discharge, because they recently encountered a similar rare case. This is an example of which cognitive bias?

options.A: Overconfidence bias
options.B: Availability bias
options.C: Commission bias only, unrelated to availability
options.D: The framing effect exclusively

questions.explanation: Availability bias occurs when a recent or memorable case distorts a clinician's estimate of probability, making a rare condition seem more likely simply because it is 'at the forefront of the mind' — exactly as described, overriding a systematic (Type 2) assessment with an irrational intuitive override.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Common Cognitive Biases

questions.question: In the 'dual process theory' of clinical reasoning, 'Type 1' thinking is best described as:

options.A: Slow, deliberate, and highly analytical
options.B: Intuitive, fast, automatic, and pattern-recognition based, but more vulnerable to error
options.C: Used exclusively by inexperienced clinicians
options.D: A thinking style with no relevance to medical practice

questions.explanation: Type 1 thinking is intuitive, heuristic, automatic, fast, and effortless — highly efficient (used in roughly 95% of daily decisions) but more vulnerable to error and more affected by context than Type 2 thinking, which is slow, deliberate, and analytical.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Type 1 and Type 2 Thinking

questions.question: The D-dimer test has high sensitivity but low specificity for pulmonary embolism. What does this mean in practice?

options.A: A positive D-dimer confirms pulmonary embolism definitively
options.B: A negative D-dimer helps rule out pulmonary embolism, but a positive result does not confirm it — it only means the disease has not been excluded
options.C: The D-dimer test is useless in clinical practice
options.D: High sensitivity and low specificity mean the test is always accurate regardless of result

questions.explanation: A highly sensitive test detects most true disease (few false negatives), so a negative result is reassuring and helps exclude the disease. But low specificity means many people without the disease will still test positive (false positives) — so a raised D-dimer does not confirm pulmonary embolism, it simply means it cannot yet be excluded, prompting further imaging.
questions.sourceBook: Davidson's Principles and Practice of Medicine
questions.sourceChapter: Clinical Decision Making — Interpreting Test Results

questions.question: The reddish vaginal discharge seen in the first 1-4 days after delivery is called:

options.A: Lochia alba
options.B: Lochia serosa
options.C: Lochia rubra
options.D: Leukorrhea

questions.explanation: Lochia progresses through three stages by colour: lochia rubra (red, days 1-4), lochia serosa (yellowish/pink/pale brownish, days 5-9), and lochia alba (pale white, days 10-15).
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Lochia

questions.question: 'Subinvolution' and 'superinvolution' of the uterus refer respectively to:

options.A: Delayed/incomplete involution, and a smaller-than-normal uterus sometimes seen with continued lactation
options.B: Two names for exactly the same clinical finding
options.C: Involution occurring only in the cervix versus only in the vagina
options.D: Terms with no real clinical distinction from normal involution

questions.explanation: Subinvolution refers to involution proceeding more slowly or incompletely than expected. Superinvolution, by contrast, describes a uterus that becomes smaller than normal, sometimes seen in lactating women — a change that reverses if lactation is withheld.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Clinical Assessment of Involution

questions.question: Immediately following delivery, the uterine fundus is about 13.5 cm above the symphysis pubis. Over the following days, it decreases in height at approximately what rate, becoming a pelvic organ by the end of the second week?

options.A: 0.25 cm every 24 hours
options.B: 1.25 cm every 24 hours
options.C: 5 cm every 24 hours
options.D: It does not decrease until 6 weeks postpartum

questions.explanation: After remaining constant for the first 24 hours, the fundal height decreases by about 1.25 cm every 24 hours, so that the uterus becomes a pelvic organ (no longer palpable abdominally) by the end of the second week postpartum, with involution slowing thereafter until the uterus is near-normal size by 6 weeks.
questions.sourceBook: Dutta's Textbook of Obstetrics
questions.sourceChapter: Normal Puerperium — Clinical Assessment of Involution

questions.question: Two-joint muscles such as the hamstrings and gastrocnemius are typically tested in mid-range rather than at full end-range during manual muscle testing. Why?

options.A: To avoid provoking a stretch reflex
options.B: Mid-range gives these muscles a more mechanically favorable length-tension relationship for the test
options.C: Two-joint muscles cannot generate any force at end range
options.D: It standardizes the time taken for every muscle test

questions.explanation: One-joint muscles are tested at end range for consistency, but two-joint muscles are tested in mid-range, where their length-tension relationship is more favorable — testing them at a mechanical disadvantage would make it hard to distinguish a true Grade 5 from a Grade 4.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: When testing hip abductor strength in a patient with an unstable knee, resistance is applied at the distal femur (just above the knee) instead of at the ankle. Using this shorter lever, what is the highest grade that can be assigned, even if the patient tolerates maximal resistance?

options.A: Grade 5
options.B: Grade 4
options.C: Grade 3
options.D: Grade 2

questions.explanation: A shorter lever (resistance near the knee rather than at the ankle) makes the test mechanically easier, so a patient who takes maximal resistance in this position can still only be graded a 4 — the longer lever at the ankle is needed to truly demonstrate Grade 5 strength, since it better reflects the functional demand of gait.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: On manual muscle testing (MMT), a muscle completes the full available range of motion against gravity alone, but the motion breaks as soon as any additional manual resistance is applied, however mild. What grade should this muscle receive?

options.A: Grade 5 (Normal)
options.B: Grade 4 (Good)
options.C: Grade 3 (Fair)
options.D: Grade 2 (Poor)

questions.explanation: Grade 3 (Fair) is an objective grade: the muscle can complete full range of motion against gravity, but cannot tolerate any added resistance without breaking. Grade 4 requires the muscle to also withstand considerable, though submaximal, resistance.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: Sharrard's postmortem motor neuron counts in poliomyelitis patients, cited in Daniels and Worthingham, found that by the time a muscle's MMT grade had fallen to 4 (Good), approximately what proportion of its motor neurons were already lost?

options.A: Less than 10%
options.B: About 25%
options.C: More than 50%
options.D: Nearly 100%

questions.explanation: Sharrard's data showed that more than half of a muscle's motor neurons were already gone by the time its MMT grade dropped to 4, which is why the text emphasizes that a 'Good' muscle already represents real, clinically significant weakness.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: For the vertebroscapular muscles (e.g., the rhomboids), resistance is preferably applied on the arm rather than directly on the scapula, their true point of insertion. Why?

options.A: It is simply easier for the therapist to grip the arm
options.B: The longer lever at the arm better reflects the functional demand of controlling the weight of the whole upper limb
options.C: The scapula moves too unpredictably to resist against
options.D: Resistance at the scapula risks skin breakdown

questions.explanation: Applying resistance on the arm uses a longer lever that more closely reflects the functional load these muscles must control (the weight of the arm), rather than testing at their literal anatomical insertion.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: A patient's gluteus medius is graded 4 (Good) on manual muscle testing. Which functional finding is consistent with this grade, per Daniels and Worthingham's discussion of why 'Good' is not always good enough?

options.A: Completely normal, symmetric gait with no compensation
options.B: A positive Trendelenburg sign during single-leg stance
options.C: Complete inability to abduct the hip against gravity
options.D: No palpable or visible muscle contraction at all

questions.explanation: Even a 'Good' (Grade 4) gluteus medius can be functionally inadequate — a positive Trendelenburg sign (contralateral pelvic drop in single-leg stance) can still appear, illustrating the gap between a manual muscle grade and real functional performance.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: The 'ceiling effect' of manual muscle testing refers to which limitation of the technique?

options.A: It cannot detect any degree of weakness whatsoever
options.B: A wide range of actual muscle force can all be labeled Grade 5 (Normal), masking real strength differences among people graded 'normal'
options.C: It systematically overestimates weakness in older adults
options.D: It is not valid for testing lower-extremity muscles

questions.explanation: Studies comparing MMT to hand-held dynamometry found knee extension forces ranging roughly from 85 to over 800 Newtons all classified as Grade 5 (Normal) by break testing. This 'ceiling effect' means MMT loses the ability to distinguish real strength differences once a muscle is already strong, so it is not recommended as a measure of progress above Grade 3.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 2: Relevance and Limitations of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: In manual muscle testing, the 'break test' is best described as:

options.A: Applying resistance throughout an actively moving joint to see when motion ceases
options.B: Bringing the part to the end of its available range and asking the patient to hold that position while the therapist tries to force ('break') it out of position
options.C: Passively moving a joint until tissue resistance is felt
options.D: Timing how long a muscle can sustain a maximal isometric hold

questions.explanation: The break test — the most commonly used MMT procedure — has the patient hold the end-range test position while the therapist applies gradually increasing resistance, attempting to 'break' the hold. The alternative 'active resistance test' (resisting throughout the motion) requires more skill and is not generally recommended because results are often equivocal.
questions.sourceBook: Daniels and Worthingham's Muscle Testing, 9th ed.
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 1: Principles of Manual Muscle Testing

questions.question: The Noble compression test is used to assess for which condition?

options.A: Iliotibial band friction syndrome
options.B: Meniscal tear
options.C: Patellofemoral syndrome
options.D: Osteochondritis dissecans

questions.explanation: The Noble compression test is used to assess for iliotibial band friction syndrome, a common cause of lateral knee pain particularly in runners.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee

questions.question: Which special test is specifically associated with assessing patellofemoral (patellar) instability?

options.A: The apprehension test
options.B: McMurray test
options.C: Hughston's plica test
options.D: The bounce home test

questions.explanation: The apprehension test is used to assess for patellar instability — the examiner laterally displaces the patella and observes for a look or feeling of apprehension from the patient, who fears the patella is about to dislocate.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee

questions.question: Why can a meniscal injury sometimes present with little or no pain or swelling, making diagnosis more difficult?

options.A: The menisci are avascular and have no nerve supply on their inner two-thirds
options.B: The menisci are the most richly innervated structures in the knee
options.C: Meniscal tears always occur alongside complete ACL rupture, masking symptoms
options.D: Meniscal tissue regenerates immediately after injury

questions.explanation: The menisci are avascular and lack nerve supply on their inner two-thirds, meaning an injury confined to this region can produce little or no pain or swelling — one reason meniscal injury can be difficult to diagnose confidently without a thorough history and examination.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Meniscus Injury

questions.question: The External Rotation Recurvatum Test, in which the examiner lifts both of the patient's big toes off the table and observes for relative hyperextension and lateral tibial rotation on the affected side, is a test for:

options.A: Posterolateral rotary instability in extension
options.B: Meniscal tear
options.C: Patellofemoral pain syndrome
options.D: Iliotibial band tightness

questions.explanation: The External Rotation Recurvatum Test assesses for posterolateral rotary instability in extension — a positive test shows the affected knee falling into relative hyperextension (genu varum appearance) with lateral tibial rotation due to gravity, when both legs are lifted by the toes.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — External Rotation Recurvatum Test

questions.question: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both special tests associated with which condition?

options.A: Patellofemoral syndrome
options.B: Iliotibial band friction syndrome
options.C: Meniscus lesions
options.D: Leg length discrepancy

questions.explanation: Clarke's sign and the McConnell test are both used in the assessment of patellofemoral syndrome (anterior knee pain related to patellar tracking/compression issues).
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee

questions.question: Using the KT-1000 arthrometer, a difference of more than 3 mm in anterior displacement between the injured and uninjured knee is generally considered:

options.A: A normal finding requiring no further action
options.B: Diagnostic for injury to the anterior or posterior cruciate ligament
options.C: Evidence of a meniscal tear specifically, never a ligament injury
options.D: Only relevant in paediatric patients

questions.explanation: A side-to-side difference of more than 3 mm in anterior displacement on KT-1000 arthrometer testing is generally considered diagnostic for injury to the anterior cruciate ligament or posterior cruciate ligament.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Ligament Testing Devices

questions.question: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) is used to assess for which type of knee instability?

options.A: Anterolateral rotary instability
options.B: Posterolateral rotary instability
options.C: Isolated medial collateral ligament sprain only
options.D: Patellofemoral instability

questions.explanation: The Jakob test (reverse pivot shift maneuver) tests for posterolateral rotary instability — a positive test (jerk in the knee, or posterior tibial shift with a 'giving way' sensation) indicates injury to the lateral collateral ligament, arcuate-popliteus complex, and mid-third of the lateral capsule.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Tests for Posterolateral Rotary Instability

questions.question: Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign is performed with the patient supine, knee flexed 80-90°, hip flexed 45°, and the foot slightly medially rotated. A positive test (excessive posterior movement/rotation of the medial tibia) is most indicative of injury to which primary structure?

options.A: Anterior cruciate ligament in isolation
options.B: Posterior cruciate ligament (along with posteromedial supporting structures)
options.C: Lateral collateral ligament only
options.D: Iliotibial band

questions.explanation: A positive Hughston's posteromedial drawer sign indicates injury to the posterior cruciate ligament, along with possible involvement of the posterior oblique ligament, medial collateral ligament, semimembranosus, and posteromedial capsule — it tests for posteromedial rotary instability of the knee.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Ligament Stability, Posteromedial and Posterolateral Drawer Sign

questions.question: In arthrometer testing, the 'quadriceps active position' refers to the knee angle at which:

options.A: The tibia shows no forward movement when the quadriceps contracts, typically around 70° of flexion
options.B: The knee is fully extended at 0°
options.C: The patient is asked to relax completely with no muscle contraction
options.D: The hamstrings are maximally contracted instead of the quadriceps

questions.explanation: The quadriceps neutral (active) angle is the knee flexion angle — typically around 70° — at which an isolated quadriceps contraction produces no anterior tibial translation in a normal knee; this position is used as a reference when testing the injured knee for abnormal anterior displacement (suggestive of PCL injury).
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Quadriceps Neutral Test

questions.question: Which two special tests are classically used to assess for a meniscal injury of the knee?

options.A: McMurray test and Apley's test
options.B: Lachman test and pivot shift test
options.C: Clarke's sign and the Q-angle measurement
options.D: Noble compression test and Ober's test

questions.explanation: The McMurray test and Apley's (compression/distraction) test are the classic special tests for meniscal injury of the knee, alongside the 'bounce home' test.
questions.sourceBook: Magee, Orthopedic Physical Assessment
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 12: Knee — Special Tests Commonly Performed on the Knee

questions.question: Middle Cerebral Artery (MCA) syndrome, the most common site of occlusion in stroke, classically produces contralateral weakness and sensory loss most affecting:

options.A: The lower extremity, sparing the face and upper extremity
options.B: The face and upper extremity, with relative sparing of the lower extremity
options.C: Only the trunk musculature
options.D: Bilateral lower extremities equally

questions.explanation: MCA syndrome classically produces contralateral spastic hemiparesis and sensory loss of the face, upper extremity, and lower extremity, with the face and upper extremity more affected than the lower extremity — the MCA is also the most common site of stroke occlusion overall.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome

questions.question: Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SH) typically results from rupture of which type of vascular lesion?

options.A: A saccular (berry) aneurysm affecting large blood vessels
options.B: Small penetrating vessel disease (lacunar disease)
options.C: Atherosclerotic plaque in the carotid artery only
options.D: Venous thrombosis in the dural sinuses exclusively

questions.explanation: Subarachnoid hemorrhage typically occurs from bleeding into the subarachnoid space, most often from rupture of a saccular (berry) aneurysm affecting the larger cerebral blood vessels, often related to congenital weakness in the vessel wall.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Pathophysiology

questions.question: By definition, a transient ischemic attack (TIA) produces focal neurological deficits that:

options.A: Last longer than 24 hours with permanent residual damage
options.B: Do not last longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual brain damage afterward
options.C: Always progress to a completed stroke within 24 hours
options.D: Only ever affect vision, never motor function

questions.explanation: A TIA is a temporary interruption of blood supply producing focal neurological deficits lasting minutes to hours but, by definition, not longer than 24 hours, with no evidence of residual damage afterward. However, TIA is clinically significant as a warning sign — about 15% of strokes are preceded by a TIA, with the highest risk in the following 90 days.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Management Categories

questions.question: The circle of Willis is clinically important in stroke because it:

options.A: Has no role in cerebral perfusion at all
options.B: Provides a collateral circulatory network that can help maintain blood flow if one contributing artery is occluded proximally
options.C: Is located exclusively in the spinal cord
options.D: Only supplies the cerebellum

questions.explanation: The circle of Willis connects the anterior and posterior cerebral circulations via communicating arteries, providing collateral blood flow. This is why occlusion proximal to the anterior or posterior communicating arteries often produces relatively minimal deficits — perfusion can be partly maintained from the other side.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Vascular Syndromes

questions.question: A stroke patient has nonfluent, slow, hesitant speech with a limited vocabulary, but relatively preserved auditory comprehension. This is classically associated with a lesion of:

options.A: Wernicke's area, in the posterior temporal gyrus
options.B: Broca's area, in the third frontal convolution of the dominant hemisphere
options.C: The primary visual cortex
options.D: The cerebellum

questions.explanation: This is classic Broca's (nonfluent, expressive) aphasia — slow, effortful, nonfluent speech with a limited vocabulary but relatively preserved comprehension — caused by a lesion of Broca's area in the dominant (typically left) frontal lobe. Wernicke's (fluent, receptive) aphasia, by contrast, produces fluent but often meaningless speech with impaired comprehension.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome

questions.question: Cerebral edema following ischemic stroke typically reaches its maximum at approximately what time point, and is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke?

options.A: Within the first hour
options.B: 3 to 4 days
options.C: 6 months
options.D: It never resolves

questions.explanation: Cerebral edema begins within minutes of the ischemic insult and reaches its maximum by 3 to 4 days, gradually subsiding by 2 to 3 weeks. Significant edema, particularly with large MCA/ICA infarcts, is the most frequent cause of death in acute stroke due to raised intracranial pressure and brainstem herniation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Pathophysiology

questions.question: Anterior Cerebral Artery (ACA) syndrome classically produces contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss that is:

options.A: Greater in the lower extremity than the upper extremity
options.B: Greater in the upper extremity and face than the lower extremity
options.C: Equal throughout the whole body with no distinguishing pattern
options.D: Limited exclusively to the face

questions.explanation: Because the ACA supplies the medial aspect of the cerebral hemisphere where the lower extremity is somatotopically represented, ACA syndrome classically produces contralateral hemiparesis and sensory loss with greater involvement of the lower extremity than the upper extremity — the opposite pattern to MCA syndrome.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Anterior Cerebral Artery Syndrome

questions.question: Lesions of the parietal lobe of the NONDOMINANT (typically right) hemisphere in MCA syndrome typically produce which type of deficit?

options.A: Aphasia (language impairment)
options.B: Perceptual deficits such as unilateral neglect, anosognosia, and spatial disorganization
options.C: Complete loss of hearing
options.D: Loss of the sense of smell only

questions.explanation: While dominant (usually left) hemisphere parieto-occipital lesions typically produce aphasia, lesions of the nondominant (usually right) parietal lobe typically produce perceptual deficits: unilateral neglect, anosognosia (denial of deficit), apraxia, and spatial disorganization.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Middle Cerebral Artery Syndrome

questions.question: Occlusion of a posterior cerebral artery (PCA), affecting the occipital lobe, characteristically produces:

options.A: Contralateral homonymous hemianopsia
options.B: Complete bilateral blindness in every case
options.C: Isolated hearing loss
options.D: Pure motor weakness with no sensory or visual involvement

questions.explanation: The PCA supplies the occipital lobe (primary visual cortex); occlusion produces contralateral homonymous hemianopsia. Bilateral PCA occlusion can cause cortical blindness, but this is not the typical single-vessel presentation.
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Posterior Cerebral Artery Syndrome

questions.question: Strokes are broadly classified into two main categories based on underlying pathology:

options.A: Ischemic and hemorrhagic
options.B: Acute and chronic only
options.C: Left-sided and right-sided
options.D: Cortical and subcortical only

questions.explanation: Strokes are broadly classified as ischemic (from thrombus, embolism, or low systemic perfusion depriving brain tissue of blood flow) or hemorrhagic (from rupture of a cerebral vessel causing bleeding into or around the brain).
questions.sourceBook: O'Sullivan, Physical Rehabilitation
questions.sourceChapter: Chapter 15: Stroke — Pathophysiology

questions.question: Stridor is often mistakenly called 'wheeze' by patients, but it actually indicates:

options.A: Upper airway obstruction
options.B: Pleural effusion
options.C: Normal breath sounds
options.D: Lower lobe consolidation only

questions.explanation: Stridor is the sound produced by upper airway obstruction and is often mistakenly labelled 'wheeze' by patients, though true wheeze arises from turbulent airflow through narrowed lower airways — an important clinical distinction.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Wheeze

questions.question: Pleuritic chest pain is best described as:

options.A: A dull, central, band-like pain radiating to the jaw
options.B: A severe, sharp, stabbing pain, worse on inspiration, and not reproduced by palpation
options.C: A burning retrosternal pain worse when lying flat or bending forward
options.D: Pain that is only ever felt during exercise and never at rest

questions.explanation: Pleuritic chest pain, from inflammation of the parietal pleura, is classically a severe, sharp, stabbing pain that worsens on inspiration and is NOT reproduced by palpation — distinguishing it from musculoskeletal chest wall pain, which IS reproduced by palpation.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Chest Pain

questions.question: Peripheral oedema in a respiratory patient most commonly suggests which underlying process?

options.A: Right heart failure, potentially due to cor pulmonale (right ventricular failure secondary to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction)
options.B: Left ventricular failure exclusively
options.C: Normal ageing with no pathological significance
options.D: Acute asthma exacerbation

questions.explanation: Peripheral oedema in a respiratory patient suggests right heart failure, which may result from cor pulmonale — right ventricular failure secondary to hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction from underlying chronic lung disease. It can also occur from salt/water retention with high-dose corticosteroid use.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Other Symptoms

questions.question: Isolated haemoptysis (coughing up blood), even when the chest radiograph appears normal, may be the first sign of which condition?

options.A: Bronchogenic carcinoma
options.B: Simple viral upper respiratory tract infection
options.C: Asthma exclusively
options.D: Hyperventilation syndrome

questions.explanation: Isolated haemoptysis can be the first sign of bronchogenic carcinoma even when the chest X-ray is normal, which is why it should always be taken seriously and investigated further rather than dismissed.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Sputum, Haemoptysis

questions.question: Morning headaches in a patient with severe respiratory failure may signify:

options.A: Nocturnal carbon dioxide retention
options.B: Simple dehydration only
options.C: Normal sleep patterns with no pathology
options.D: Acute pulmonary embolism specifically

questions.explanation: Morning headaches in patients with severe respiratory failure may signify nocturnal carbon dioxide retention (hypercapnia during sleep), which can be confirmed with early morning arterial blood gases or nocturnal transcutaneous CO2 monitoring.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Other Symptoms

questions.question: 'Rusty' coloured sputum is classically associated with infection by which organism?

options.A: Pseudomonas
options.B: Pneumococcus
options.C: Haemophilus
options.D: Klebsiella

questions.explanation: Rusty-coloured sputum is a classic finding associated with pneumococcal infection (typical lobar pneumonia), whereas dark green/brown sputum suggests Pseudomonas, and 'red-currant jelly' sputum suggests Klebsiella.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Sputum

questions.question: Angina pectoris from myocardial ischaemia is classically described as:

options.A: A sharp, localized pain that worsens specifically on inspiration
options.B: A dull, central, retrosternal gripping or band-like sensation that may radiate to the arm, neck, or jaw
options.C: A superficial pain reproduced by chest wall palpation
options.D: A pain confined strictly to the left shoulder with no central component

questions.explanation: Angina pectoris characteristically produces a dull, central, retrosternal gripping or band-like sensation, which may radiate to either arm, the neck, or the jaw — quite distinct from the sharp, localized, movement/palpation-related pain of musculoskeletal chest pain.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Chest Pain

questions.question: On the Glasgow Coma Scale, what is the maximum total score, and what does it represent?

options.A: 10, representing moderate impairment
options.B: 15, representing a fully alert, orientated patient
options.C: 3, the best possible score
options.D: 100, on a percentage-based scale

questions.explanation: The Glasgow Coma Scale has a maximum total score of 15 (best possible — eye opening 4, verbal response 5, motor response 6), representing full alertness, and a minimum score of 3, representing the deepest level of unresponsiveness.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Objective Assessment, Coma Scale

questions.question: A daily, chronic productive cough is described as a fundamental feature of which conditions?

options.A: Interstitial lung disease
options.B: Chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis
options.C: Pulmonary embolism
options.D: Asthma exclusively

questions.explanation: A chronic productive cough occurring every day is a fundamental feature of chronic bronchitis and bronchiectasis, whereas interstitial lung disease is characteristically associated with a persistent DRY cough.
questions.sourceBook: Pryor & Prasad, Physiotherapy for Respiratory and Cardiac Problems
questions.sourceChapter: Assessment — Cough

questions.question: How is musculoskeletal (chest wall) pain typically distinguished from pleuritic pain on physical examination?

options.A: Musculoskeletal pain is reproduced by palpation, while pleuritic pain is not
